description: A two-minute surf-tinged storm from Pixies' 1989 album Doolittle, where Black Francis drives into the ocean and sails away into one of alternative rock's prettiest, darkest choruses.

pops.text: Track three on Doolittle, released April 17, 1989. Pixies tucked this ocean-going oddity right after 'Tame,' early proof the album had range.
Written and sung by frontman Black Francis. Producer Gil Norton gave Doolittle a clean, polished sound that makes its violent, surreal songs hit even harder.
Francis said the lyric grew from stories of Japanese businessmen who, after failing in business, drove their families off a pier into the ocean.
AllMusic clocked it at just over two minutes — yet it still squeezes in several tempo changes. Classic Pixies: no wasted seconds.
That propulsive pulse underneath is Kim Deal's bass, driving the song while Joey Santiago's guitar buzzes around the vocal melody.
'Could find my way to Mariana' points to the Mariana Trench, the deepest part of the world's oceans. Even the geography here goes deep.
Francis called the song gentle and dreamy — almost un-Pixies-like. Drummer David Lovering even used mallets on the drums for its softer feel.
The band cut a second take on it: the slower 'UK Surf' version, released as the B-side of the 'Here Comes Your Man' single in 1989.
That UK Surf version swam into movies — it is on the Pump Up the Volume soundtrack (1990) and later turned up in Southland Tales (2006).
The song was so defining that Pixies' 2004 greatest-hits album was named after it: Wave of Mutilation: Best of Pixies.

title: Wave of Mutilation

description: Ninety seconds, three verses and two fictional delinquents: Joey Ramone's mini-saga from the Ramones' 1976 debut, and one of the shortest, sharpest blueprints for punk rock ever recorded.

pops.text: Track three on Ramones, the debut album released April 23, 1976 on Sire Records. Punk rock, reduced to its absolute essentials.
At about 1 minute 30 seconds, it is the shortest song on the debut album. Blink and Jackie and Judy are already in Berlin.
Joey Ramone wrote it. He said the first line came to him walking past Thorny Croft, a Forest Hills apartment building where neighborhood kids hung out on the roof.
Jackie and Judy are fictional juvenile delinquents — in verse one they go down to Berlin and join the Ice Capades. As one does.
Hear that announcement? 'Second verse, same as the first' is a wink to Herman's Hermits' 1965 hit 'I'm Henry VIII, I Am,' which does the same trick.
Third verse, different from the first: now the pair head to San Francisco — 'Frisco' — to join the S.L.A., the Symbionese Liberation Army.
An early demo of this song was recorded September 19, 1975 at 914 Sound Studios — the demo that helped land Ramones their Sire Records deal.
The debut album itself was recorded in about seven days for roughly $6,400, produced by Craig Leon. Cheap, fast and loud was the whole point.
Jackie and Judy lived again: Ramones brought them back in 'The Return of Jackie and Judy' on the 1980 album End of the Century.
Full-circle fan: Morrissey panned Ramones in a 1976 letter, later curated a Ramones compilation in 2014, then covered this very song live in New York in 2016.

title: Judy Is a Punk

description: Ramones' angriest single: a 1985 UK-only protest against Ronald Reagan's visit to a German war cemetery, so pointed that the band retitled it for their own album a year later.

pops.text: Released as a UK single in June 1985 on Beggars Banquet. It never got a U.S. single release — America had to buy the import.
The trigger: on May 5, 1985, President Ronald Reagan visited the military cemetery at Bitburg, West Germany, where Waffen-SS soldiers were buried.
Joey Ramone, who was Jewish, said he was disgusted by the visit. He co-wrote the song with Dee Dee Ramone and producer Jean Beauvoir.
'Bonzo' was Reagan's nickname from his movie days: he starred with a chimp in the 1951 comedy Bedtime for Bonzo.
The title riffs on that film's sequel, Bonzo Goes to College (1952) — though Reagan was not actually in the sequel.
Producer Jean Beauvoir came to Ramones from the Plasmatics. Animal Boy, the album this landed on, was his first of several productions for the band.
As an import, the single became a hit on U.S. college radio — students were spinning a protest record their own country would not release.
Band politics in one title: guitarist Johnny Ramone was a staunch Reagan supporter, so for the 1986 album Animal Boy it was retitled 'My Brain Is Hanging Upside Down.'
The original title survived only in parentheses on the album: 'My Brain Is Hanging Upside Down (Bonzo Goes to Bitburg).'
New generation, same headache: the studio version was used in the 2003 film School of Rock, under its full parenthetical title.

title: Bonzo Goes to Bitburg

description: Rebirth Brass Band's signature party anthem from their 1989 Rounder era — a second-line call to do exactly what the title says, written by three high-school friends from Tremé.

pops.text: Written by Kermit Ruffins with brothers Keith and Philip Frazier — the three teenagers who founded Rebirth in 1983 at Joseph S. Clark High School in Tremé.
Ruffins told WFUV it is his favorite of his own songs: 'The most special time of my life, and I didn't realize I was writing a hit.'
The title came from the street: Ruffins told WWOZ that neighborhood guys were always saying, 'I'm gonna do what I wanna!'
It first spread on the band's 1989 Rounder album Feel Like Funkin' It Up, where 'Do Whatcha Wanna, Pt. 2' was produced by Ron Levy.
Listen for the whole parade in the recording: tambourines, cowbells, handclaps and crowd noise are built right into the track.
The groove rides the classic second-line pattern — horns and drums trading call-and-response over a 3+3+2 rhythm.
Ruffins swears the tune feels older than the band: he thinks of it as an old, old Mardi Gras standard that was somehow always there.
It became so central that Rebirth named a whole album after it: Do Whatcha Wanna, released on Mardi Gras Records in 1991.
Rebirth cut it while reinventing the brass band for a young audience, mixing second-line tradition with funk, soul and early hip-hop energy.
Decades on, it remains a New Orleans party staple — and Rebirth themselves won the 2012 Grammy for Best Regional Roots Music Album.

title: Do Whatcha Wanna

description: The lead single from Exile on Main St. (1972), cut in a French villa basement by tax exiles: a loose boogie groove about a gambler who cannot stay faithful. It took dozens of takes — and became a permanent Stones concert staple.

pops.text: First roll: released worldwide on April 14, 1972 as the lead single from Exile on Main St., with 'Sweet Black Angel' on the B-side. It was the Stones' 23rd US single.

It started faster: an early version called 'Good Time Women' was recorded in 1970 during the Sticky Fingers sessions at Stargroves. That take finally surfaced as a bonus track on the 2010 deluxe Exile reissue.
Tax-exile rock: the band had fled Britain's 93 per cent supertax for southern France, recording at odd hours in the basement of the Villa Nellcôte near Villefranche-sur-Mer.

Upstairs, downstairs: Keith Richards wrote the riff in the villa's elegant front room and took it down to the basement the same evening to cut it. He played it with a capo on the fourth fret in his five-string open-G 'Keef-chord' tuning.
Musical chairs on the basic track, cut August 3, 1971: with Bill Wyman absent, guitarist Mick Taylor played bass and Mick Jagger played rhythm guitar.

Engineer Andy Johns called recording it 'like pulling teeth' — he counted between thirty and a hundred reels of tape for the basic track, with some estimates reaching 150 takes. Jagger has never liked the final mix.
Homework in Los Angeles: finishing the song at Sunset Sound, Jagger completed the gambling lyrics after talking with a housekeeper who liked to play dice — a subject he admitted he knew little about.

Two drummers, sort of: producer Jimmy Miller plays drums as the coda begins, where Charlie Watts was having trouble. It is the only Stones song where Watts overdubbed a second drum track over the original.
Chart roll: No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the US and No. 5 in the UK, where it spent eight weeks on the chart. It also made the top 10 in the Netherlands, Norway and Spain.

Covered and canonised: Linda Ronstadt's version on her 1977 album Simple Dreams became a Top 40 single the next year. Rolling Stone ranked the Stones' original No. 86 on its 2021 list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.

title: Tumbling Dice

description: A funk-rock deep cut from Blood Sugar Sex Magik, sitting at track 12 right after 'Under the Bridge.' Kiedis sings a love letter to animals — killer whales and elephants included — over Flea's bouncing bass.

pops.text: Sequencing whiplash: this is track 12 on Blood Sugar Sex Magik, placed immediately after the quiet ache of 'Under the Bridge.' The album recovers loudly.
Early bird: 'Naked in the Rain' was among the first songs the band wrote for the album, and they played it once at the end of the Mother's Milk tour in 1990.
Full-band credit: like the album's other originals, it was written by all four Chili Peppers — Kiedis, Flea, John Frusciante and Chad Smith.
The album was recorded at The Mansion in Los Angeles in spring 1991, with most of the band living in the house while they worked.
Chad Smith skipped the sleepover: the drummer didn't stay at The Mansion and instead arrived each day by motorcycle.
Gear nerds, listen for the wah: Frusciante played his Ibanez WH10 wah pedal in its bass mode on this track — a guitar effect, set for the low end.
The lyric is a wildlife fan letter: 'I never met an animal that I didn't like,' Kiedis declares, before asking Doctor Doolittle for his secret.
Flea was on a less-is-more kick for this album, saying he tried to play half as many notes so that when he did play something busy, it stood out.
The Mansion sessions were filmed by Flea's brother-in-law, and the footage became the band's 1991 documentary, Funky Monks.
It was never a single — the album's five singles were other songs — but it got a second life in 2008 as Rock Band downloadable content with the full album pack.

title: Naked in the Rain

description: Recorded for Blood Sugar Sex Magik, left off the album, then rescued by the Coneheads soundtrack in 1993. The leftover became a No. 1 modern-rock hit — not bad for a B-side.

pops.text: This was recorded during the Blood Sugar Sex Magik sessions in 1991 — and then left off the album entirely. The outtake drawer held gold.
Its first life was as a B-side, tucked onto the singles for both 'Give It Away' and 'Under the Bridge' before anyone called it a hit.
Under the dreamy surface, Kiedis's opening verse details his struggle with addiction — a theme American Songwriter singles out in the song.
Release day, finally: it came out as a single on August 17, 1993, tied to the Coneheads film soundtrack.
Chart squeeze: No. 1 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks, No. 7 on Album Rock Tracks and No. 22 on the Hot 100.
World tour by chart: it reached the top 10 in Australia, Canada, Iceland and New Zealand, and in Sweden it was the band's first single to chart at all, at No. 13.
Director Kevin Kerslake shot the video in black and white at a traveling circus, with the band members playing various sideshow 'freaks.'
Spot the Coneheads nod: Chris Farley makes a cameo in the video, one of several references to the film the song was soundtrack-ing.
Missing guitarist: John Frusciante does not appear in the video. He had left the band more than a year before it was filmed, though he plays on the recording.
Vindication, eventually: the song was re-released on the band's 2003 Greatest Hits album, an official promotion from B-side to best-of.

title: Soul to Squeeze

description: From Plant's second solo album, The Principle of Moments (1983): a dreamy, floating groove co-written with his new bandmates. Phil Collins is on drums — yes, that Phil Collins.

pops.text: Solo album number two: this is from The Principle of Moments, released July 15, 1983, Plant's follow-up to his solo debut, Pictures at Eleven.
It's track two on the album, and a team write: Plant co-wrote it with guitarist Robbie Blunt and bassist Paul Martinez, his post-Zeppelin bandmates.
That drummer is Phil Collins. The Genesis man played on this track and on five of the album's eight songs in total.
Collins didn't just record it — he drummed on the North American leg of Plant's 1983 tour, content to sit in the background despite his own huge solo success.
Big shoes department: Blunt had stepped into the guitar-foil role previously occupied by Jimmy Page, and co-wrote every song on the album.
Physics homework: the album title refers to the principle of moments — Varignon's theorem, about how the moment of a force equals the sum of its components' moments.
Label boss, too: The Principle of Moments was the first release on Plant's own Es Paranza Records, after Led Zeppelin's Swan Song label folded.
Radio found it first: as an album track it reached No. 4 on Billboard's Top Tracks chart before it was ever released as a single.
As a single it entered the Hot 100 on November 19, 1983, and peaked at No. 39 in January 1984 — Plant's second solo Top 40 hit, after 'Big Log.' In the UK it reached No. 81.
The 2007 Rhino remaster added a live version as a bonus track, taken from the live tapes recorded at The Summit in Houston on September 20, 1983.

title: In the Mood

description: Plant's first solo Top 40 hit: a hushed, drum-machine-driven road song from The Principle of Moments. Neither 'big' nor 'log' appears in the lyrics — the title came from an actual log.

pops.text: First out of the gate: 'Big Log' was the first single from The Principle of Moments, released in July 1983 ahead of the album.
Plant wrote it with Robbie Blunt and keyboardist Jezz Woodroffe, and it was recorded at Rockfield Studios in Monmouth, Wales.
That steady pulse is a machine: Woodroffe recalled messing about with a Roland TR-808 drum machine and coming up with the drum pattern and hand claps.
Woodroffe's Godwin string synth supplied the middle eight, and Blunt arrived with the haunting guitar theme. The groove came together very quickly, by their account.
Title origin: written mid-winter, the writers ran out of fire fuel, found a roughly 15-foot tree trunk outside with nothing to cut it, and fed one end into the fire until it hollowed.
Sing along carefully: neither of the words in the title — 'big' or 'log' — appears anywhere in the lyrics.
It became Plant's first solo Top 40 hit: No. 11 in the UK, No. 20 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 6 on Billboard's Top Tracks chart.
Cash Box magazine compared the synthesized drums and claps to Marvin Gaye's 'Sexual Healing' — and praised Plant's vocal while it was at it.
Storm Thorgerson directed the video, a desert road trip filmed around California and Nevada: the Amargosa Opera House, Calico Ghost Town and Las Vegas's Glass Pool Inn.
Full-circle cover: bassist Viktor Krauss cut it in 2004 with his sister Alison Krauss singing lead — three years before she and Plant made Raising Sand together.

title: Big Log

description: Sade's international breakthrough: a bossa-tinged portrait of a jet-set con man, from the band's debut album Diamond Life. It only reached No. 19 at home — America took it to No. 5.

pops.text: Old song, new band: Sade Adu co-wrote this in 1982 with Ray St. John while both were still in their previous band, Pride — and it sat unrecorded.
It was the third UK single from debut album Diamond Life, released August 28, 1984, with 'Spirit' as the B-side; the 12-inch added 'Red Eye.'
It was recorded in 1983 at London's Power Plant studio, produced by Robin Millar — the same team behind the whole Diamond Life album.
That opening is spoken, not sung: Adu's spoken recitation is a signature of the song, though some radio edits cut it and jumped straight to the singing.
The operator's itinerary is the lyric: coast to coast, Los Angeles to Chicago, with a heart described as cold as ice and a jet-set life to match.
The slinky saxophone comes from within the band: Stuart Matthewman, Sade's saxophonist and guitarist, is one of its four core members.
Julien Temple directed the noir nightclub video — the operator is played by Michael Feast, with Amanda Pays as the waitress. Temple later cast Adu in his 1986 film Absolute Beginners.
The extended video, incorporating 'Red Eye,' goes full crime film: working with the police, Adu gives herself away, and the operator flees across rooftops before being shot and falling.
America got it: released in the US in February 1985, it peaked at No. 5 on the Hot 100 for two weeks and topped the Adult Contemporary chart for two weeks. The UK peak was No. 19.
The video earned two nominations at the 1985 MTV Video Music Awards — Best Female Video and Best New Artist in a Video — helping make it the band's signature song.

title: Smooth Operator

description: The lead single from Sade's second album Promise (1985): a silky quiet-storm groove written by Sade Adu and Martin Ditcham that climbed to No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped the US Adult Contemporary chart.

pops.text: Lead single from Sade's second album, Promise, released in October 1985 and written by Sade Adu with the band's guitarist, Martin Ditcham.
The album's title came from a letter written by Adu's father, who spoke of a promise of hope while he was battling cancer.
Producer Robin Millar keeps everything unhurried — this is quiet storm at its smoothest, all groove and no raised voices. The track runs 4:37.
The flip side of the original single was 'You're Not the Man.'
America fell hard: the song spent six months on the Billboard Hot 100, 13 of those weeks inside the Top 40.
In March 1986 it peaked at No. 5 on the Hot 100, and it reached No. 3 on Billboard's R&B chart.
It also topped Billboard's Adult Contemporary chart — Sade's second straight AC No. 1, right after 'Smooth Operator'.
Britain, oddly, shrugged: for all its US success, the single stalled at just No. 31 on the UK chart.
The video, directed by Brian Ward, cuts between the band playing in a New York City loft and desert scenes shot in Andalusia, Spain.

To be continued: the video's storyline picks up again in the clip for the follow-up single, 'Is It a Crime?' Meanwhile Promise hit No. 1 in the UK and US, went four-times platinum in America, and Sade won the 1986 Grammy for Best New Artist.

title: The Sweetest Taboo

description: Title track of Soulive's 2001 Blue Note debut: a six-minute organ-trio workout written by guitarist Eric Krasno, powered by brothers Alan and Neal Evans and dressed up with horn arrangements from James Brown trombonist Fred Wesley.

pops.text: Soulive began as a jam: on March 2, 1999, brothers Alan and Neal Evans invited guitarist Eric Krasno to their Woodstock, New York home studio. That session became their first EP, Get Down!
There's no bass player in this band — Neal Evans covers the low end on the bass keys of his Hammond B-3 organ, while brother Alan drives the drums.
This is the title track of the trio's first album for Blue Note Records, released March 13, 2001 — their third record overall, and the major-label leap.
Eric Krasno wrote this one, and it runs 6:46. Soulive songs are built to stretch out.
Their 2000 indie album Turn It Out — with a guest spot from John Scofield — created such a buzz that Blue Note signed the band that fall.
Hear the extra muscle? For this album the trio added a four-piece brass section, arranged by trombonist Fred Wesley.
Wesley's résumé is funk royalty: he was James Brown's trombonist, played on 'Say It Loud – I'm Black and I'm Proud,' and co-wrote the JB's classic 'Hot Pants.'
The album peaked at No. 14 on Billboard's Jazz Albums chart — jam-band energy, charting in the jazz world.
Elsewhere on the record: vocalist Stephanie McKay's showcase 'Romantic,' and 'Evidence' — a Thelonious Monk title hiding inside a funk album.
In 2010 the trio started Bowlive, their guest-packed residency at Brooklyn Bowl — proof that the 'something' they started doin' in Woodstock never really stopped.

title: Doin' Something

description: An Alan Evans composition tucked at track nine of Soulive's Blue Note debut, Doin' Something (2001). The organ trio locks into a tight, no-frills funk groove — solid by name, solid by nature.

pops.text: Track nine: 'Solid' sits near the end of Doin' Something, Soulive's 2001 Blue Note debut, and runs just under five minutes — 4:53 on the album.
The drummer wrote it: Alan Evans is the track's sole credited composer, while his brother Neal works the Hammond B-3 and Eric Krasno plays guitar.
Doin' Something was Soulive's first album for Blue Note, released March 13, 2001, after their indie album Turn It Out created the buzz that got them signed.
The band was born at a jam: a March 2, 1999 session in Woodstock, New York became their debut EP, Get Down!, and launched the trio.
No bassist, no problem: Neal Evans covers the bass lines himself, hammering them out with his left hand and his feet on the Hammond organ.
For this album the trio expanded: Doin' Something added a four-piece brass section led by Fred Wesley, James Brown's legendary trombonist.
The album reached No. 14 on Billboard's Jazz Albums chart — a strong showing for a groove trio on a major jazz label.
Behind the desk: the album was produced by Jeff Krasno, Bob Brockmann and Yaron Fuchs, with Brockmann and Fuchs also handling mixing and recording.
'Solid' got a second life on stage: a stretched-out 6:12 live version is track three on the 2003 live album Soulive, which peaked at No. 10 on Billboard's jazz chart.
It's a deep cut's deep cut: a 2002 jambands.com review called 'Solid' rarely performed, and setlist.fm statistics count just five live performances.

title: Solid

description: Speedometer's instrumental Northern-soul take on Pharrell Williams' 'Happy' — recorded just for fun, launched on YouTube, and so heavily requested that Freestyle Records had to release it as a single in 2014.

pops.text: Yes, that 'Happy': this is an instrumental cover of Pharrell Williams' Despicable Me 2 smash, rebuilt as a gritty soul-jazz and Northern soul groove.
It was never meant to be a single: the band recorded it 'just for fun' and launched it on YouTube, according to its label, Freestyle Records.
The internet demanded it: the video quickly amassed viewings and generated request after request for it to be fully released, the label says.
Release day: Freestyle issued it as a digital single on February 28, 2014, catalogue number FSRSPEEDIG01, running 3:37.
By 2017 the video was closing on 500,000 YouTube views, and the track had enjoyed weeks of regular radio airplay, per the band's event biographies.
One reviewer summed up the sound as Grant Green meets Ramsey Lewis via Al Kent — classic soul-jazz guitar and piano through a Northern soul filter.
The band behind it: Speedometer formed in 1999 in southeast England as an instrumental quartet paying homage to The Meters and The JB's.
They are led by guitarist Leigh Gracie, and in 2001 they expanded, adding the highly regarded horn section and vocalists behind their powerhouse deep-funk sound.
Speedometer are a backing band of choice for visiting US legends — they have played behind Sharon Jones, Lee Fields, Marva Whitney, Eddie Bo and Sir Joe Quarterman.
Album afterlife: 'Happy' later took centre stage on No Turning Back, released July 24, 2015, where it was one of only two instrumentals among singer James Junior's vocal tracks.

title: Happy

description: A swaggering funk instrumental from Speedometer's KPM library album Downtown Funk 74 (2016). Made as production music for film and TV, it eventually found a spotlight as a needle drop in Hacks.

pops.text: This is library music: 'Who's the Daddy Now' comes from Downtown Funk 74, a production-music album Speedometer made for KPM — music written to be licensed into film and TV.
The album evidence: YouTube's official Topic upload credits the track to Downtown Funk 74, ℗ 2016 KPM Music Ltd, provided to YouTube by The Orchard Enterprises.
Catalogue number KPM 2008: in KPM's digital album listings, Downtown Funk 74 is dated 2016, ahead of its wider streaming release on January 13, 2017.
Its album-mates have equally no-nonsense titles — 'Tomahawk,' 'Gumbo Ya Ya,' 'Jungle Fury,' 'Do the Walk' and 'Too Heavy for the Levee,' all issued by KPM Main Series on the same day.
KPM is library-music royalty: the initials stand for Keith-Prowse-Maurice, and its composers' music was written for use as signature tunes and incidental music in film and television.
KPM's roots run deep: the firm traces back to the Keith, Prowse & Co. partnership established in 1830, and EMI bought the KPM group in 1969 while keeping the famous name.
The band: Speedometer are a UK deep-funk outfit formed in 1999 in the southeast of England, led by guitarist Leigh Gracie.
They started as an instrumental quartet honouring The Meters and The JB's, then added a horn section and vocalists in 2001 to build their powerhouse sound.
Outside the library world, Speedometer's own albums come out on Freestyle Records, and they have backed visiting legends including Sharon Jones, Lee Fields and Marva Whitney.
Its moment in the spotlight: NME lists 'Who's The Daddy Now' as a needle drop in episode nine of Hacks' fifth and final season — alongside another Speedometer cut from the same album, 'Tomahawk.'

title: Who's the Daddy Now
